title: Biomolecules
tagline: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids — the four families and the chemistry that joins them.

overview.intro: Biomolecules is the chemistry chapter of the biology course, and it is examined in a very regular way: identify a class of compound from its properties, compare two classes in a table, describe the structure of an amino acid or a nucleotide, or explain the levels at which protein structure is organised. This chapter treats the four major groups in turn — carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids — then the enzymes that make the reactions of life possible, and closes with the way these molecules fit together into the cell.

facts.label: Four major groups
facts.value: Carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids, each built from a small set of repeating units.

facts.label: Amino acid
facts.value: An amino group and a carboxyl group attached to the same carbon, which also carries a hydrogen and a variable R group.

facts.label: Levels of protein structure
facts.value: Primary is the amino acid sequence, secondary is the local folding, tertiary is the full 3-D shape, quaternary is the assembly of several chains.

facts.label: DNA and RNA
facts.value: DNA is a double helix of deoxyribonucleotides carrying hereditary information; RNA is usually single-stranded and carries it to the ribosome.

learningOutcomes: Classify carbohydrates into monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides with examples and roles.
Describe the structure of a fatty acid, triglyceride, amino acid and nucleotide.
Explain the four levels of protein structure and the nature of the peptide bond.
Compare DNA and RNA under structure, sugar, bases and function.
Describe enzyme action, the factors affecting it and the modes of enzyme inhibition.

blocks.text: Carbohydrates are the compounds of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in the approximate ratio of one carbon to two hydrogen to one oxygen, written CH2O in its simplest form, and they serve as the chief source of energy in most organisms as well as a structural material. Monosaccharides are the simplest sugars and cannot be hydrolysed further: glucose, C6H12O6, is the universal respiratory substrate and occurs in blood as blood sugar; fructose is the sweet sugar of fruit; galactose is the sugar released when lactose is digested; and ribose and deoxyribose are the sugars of RNA and DNA. Disaccharides form when two monosaccharides join by a glycosidic bond with the loss of a water molecule: sucrose is glucose plus fructose and is the transport sugar in plants, maltose is two glucoses and appears during starch digestion, and lactose is glucose plus galactose and is the sugar of milk. Polysaccharides are long chains and are either storage or structural. Starch, the storage polysaccharide of plants, is a mixture of amylose, an unbranched helical chain of glucose units, and amylopectin, a branched chain with additional branch points; glycogen is the more highly branched storage polysaccharide of animals, found in liver and muscle and able to release glucose quickly; cellulose is the structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls, built of beta-glucose units joined by beta-1,4 bonds that human enzymes cannot hydrolyse, so it passes as dietary fibre; and chitin is the structural polysaccharide of the arthropod exoskeleton with N-acetylglucosamine units. Lipids are a heterogeneous group that shares insolubility in water and solubility in organic solvents. A triglyceride is formed from one molecule of glycerol, a three-carbon alcohol, and three fatty acids by esterification with the loss of three water molecules; each fatty acid has a long hydrocarbon chain with a carboxyl group at one end, and the chains may be saturated, holding no double bonds and packing tightly into solids, or unsaturated, holding one or more double bonds that kink the chain and keep the substance liquid — which is why vegetable oils are liquid at room temperature and animal fats are solid. Because the hydrocarbon chains store more than twice the energy per gram that carbohydrates do, and release water when oxidised, lipids are ideal long-term energy reserves as well as the material of membranes, where phospholipids and cholesterol appear, of insulating fat beneath the skin, and of protective cushions around organs.

Lipids are insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents, which is how they are identified.
A triglyceride is glycerol plus three fatty acids, joined by esterification with loss of water.
Saturated fatty acids pack into solids; unsaturated chains kink and keep oils liquid.
Lipids store more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrates, insulate and cushion, and form membranes.

blocks.text: Proteins are the most versatile of the biomolecules, performing structural work as collagen and keratin, catalysis as enzymes, transport as haemoglobin and membrane carriers, defence as antibodies and coordination as peptide hormones. They are polymers of amino acids, and all twenty amino acids share the same backbone: a central alpha carbon to which are attached an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and a variable side chain called the R group, which is the only part that differs and which determines the character of the amino acid — some R groups are acidic, some basic, some polar and some non-polar and hydrophobic. Two amino acids join by a condensation reaction in which the carboxyl group of one loses a hydroxyl and the amino group of the other loses a hydrogen, forming a peptide bond with the release of water; a chain of two is a dipeptide, of many a polypeptide, and a polypeptide becomes a functional protein only when folded correctly. Protein structure is organised in four levels. The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in the chain, held by peptide bonds, and it is determined by the gene — a single change, as in the altered haemoglobin of sickle-cell anaemia, can change the whole protein’s behaviour. The secondary structure is local folding into regular patterns held by hydrogen bonds between the backbone atoms: the alpha helix, a right-handed coil, and the beta pleated sheet, in which strands lie side by side. The tertiary structure is the full three-dimensional shape of a single polypeptide, held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds between charged R groups, disulphide bridges between cysteine residues and hydrophobic interactions that pull non-polar groups into the interior — and it is this shape that forms the active site of an enzyme. The quaternary structure exists only where several polypeptides assemble: haemoglobin has four chains, each with its own heme group, and collagen is a triple helix of three chains. Denaturation is the loss of the higher levels of structure through heat, extreme pH or heavy metal ions, which disrupts the bonds holding the shape; the sequence is usually untouched, but the protein loses its function because the active site no longer fits, which is why an egg turns opaque when boiled.

items: Amino acids share an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a variable R group on one carbon.
The peptide bond forms by condensation between the carboxyl of one amino acid and the amino of the next.
Primary structure is the sequence, held by peptide bonds and fixed by the gene.
Secondary structure is the alpha helix and beta pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds to the backbone.
Tertiary structure is the 3-D shape, held by hydrogen, ionic, disulphide and hydrophobic interactions.
Quaternary structure is the assembly of several polypeptides, as in haemoglobin and collagen.
Denaturation destroys higher structure through heat, pH or heavy metals and so destroys function.
Enzymes depend on their tertiary structure for the shape of the active site.

blocks.text: Nucleic acids carry the information of life, and both DNA and RNA are built from nucleotides. A nucleotide has three parts: a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and a phosphate group, joined with the phosphate esterified to the sugar and the base attached to its first carbon. The bases are of two kinds: purines with a double ring, adenine and guanine, and pyrimidines with a single ring, cytosine, thymine and uracil. DNA uses deoxyribose and holds adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine, while RNA uses ribose and holds adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil in place of thymine. DNA is a double helix of two antiparallel polynucleotide strands wound about a common axis, with sugar-phosphate backbones outside and the bases inward, where adenine pairs with thymine by two hydrogen bonds and guanine with cytosine by three — the pairing rule that makes replication possible, since each strand serves as a template for a new complementary strand. RNA is usually single-stranded and comes in three forms: messenger RNA carries the sequence from DNA to the ribosome, transfer RNA brings amino acids with its anticodon, and ribosomal RNA forms part of the ribosome itself. Enzymes are biological catalysts, almost always proteins, that speed reactions by factors of thousands without being consumed, and they do so by lowering the activation energy needed to reach the transition state. Each enzyme has an active site, a three-dimensional cleft formed by the tertiary structure of the protein, into which the substrate fits in the lock and key manner, and the enzyme-substrate complex then yields enzyme and products with the enzyme unchanged. The rate of an enzyme reaction depends on temperature, pH, substrate concentration and enzyme concentration: rising temperature increases kinetic collisions up to a point, beyond which the enzyme denatures; each enzyme has an optimum pH, near neutral for most body enzymes, strongly acidic for pepsin in the stomach and alkaline for trypsin in the intestine; and increasing substrate concentration raises the rate until every active site is occupied, at which point the enzyme is saturated and the rate levels off. Inhibition is of two kinds. Competitive inhibition uses a molecule similar in shape to the substrate that occupies the active site and blocks it, and its effect is overcome by raising the substrate concentration. Non-competitive inhibition binds elsewhere on the enzyme, changing the shape of the active site so the substrate no longer fits, and raising the substrate concentration does not help.

Base pairing is A with T by two hydrogen bonds and G with C by three.
Messenger, transfer and ribosomal RNA carry the message, the amino acid and the machine.
Enzymes lower activation energy, are not consumed and work through an active site.
Rate rises with temperature to an optimum and then falls as the enzyme denatures.
Each enzyme has an optimum pH: pepsin acidic, trypsin alkaline, most body enzymes near neutral.

learn.title: Identifying the classes and how they assemble

blocks.text: Because the four groups are distinguished by their chemistry, each can be identified by a simple test, and the sequence of tests is a standard practical question. Reducing sugars are shown by Benedict’s reagent: the sugar is heated with the blue copper sulphate solution, and a brick-red precipitate of copper oxide shows that the sugar reduces the copper — glucose gives it, sucrose does not, until sucrose is first hydrolysed, which distinguishes the reducing from the non-reducing sugar. Starch is shown by the iodine test, in which a blue-black colour appears immediately because iodine becomes trapped in the helical structure of the amylose. Proteins are shown by the biuret test, where an alkaline copper solution turns violet in the presence of peptide bonds, and by the xanthoproteic test, where concentrated nitric acid gives a yellow colour with the aromatic rings of certain amino acids. Fats are shown by the emulsion test, in which the lipid is dissolved in alcohol and the solution is poured into water to give a milky emulsion. The tests work because the classes differ in what their molecules are made of, and the same logic runs the other way: the way the monomers assemble explains the polymers. Sugars join by a glycosidic bond formed in a condensation that removes water, so hydrolysis with dilute acid reverses the process and the bond is what a disaccharide test detects. Amino acids join by a peptide bond formed the same way, so proteins are hydrolysed back to their amino acids by boiling in acid — which is how a protein digest is analysed. Nucleotides join by phosphodiester bonds forming the sugar-phosphate backbone, and it is the sequence of bases along that backbone that carries the information. Lipids differ in assembly altogether: they are built by esterification rather than polymerisation, which is why they are not true polymers and why they give no biuret or iodine response. Every classification question can therefore be answered twice — by the test that identifies the compound and by the bond that holds it together.

items: Reducing sugar: Benedict’s reagent with heat gives a brick-red precipitate.
Starch: iodine turns blue-black because iodine fits inside the amylose helix.
Protein: the biuret test turns violet in the presence of peptide bonds.
Fat: the emulsion test gives a milky cloud when the alcohol solution is diluted with water.
Condensation joins monomers and hydrolysis reverses it — the two reactions are paired.
Peptide and glycosidic bonds are broken by boiling acid, which is how digests are analysed.
Nucleotides are linked by phosphodiester bonds into a sugar-phosphate backbone.
Lipids are esters rather than polymers, which is why they behave differently in every test.

keyPoints: Carbohydrates contain carbon, hydrogen and oxygen in about 1:2:1 and provide energy and structure.
Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed; disaccharides join two with a glycosidic bond; polysaccharides are long chains.
Starch and glycogen are storage polysaccharides; cellulose and chitin are structural.
Lipids are insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvents and store twice the energy per gram of sugars.
A triglyceride is glycerol plus three fatty acids joined by esterification.
Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds formed in condensation reactions.
Protein structure has four levels: primary sequence, secondary folding, tertiary shape and quaternary assembly.
Denaturation removes higher structure and with it function, leaving the sequence intact.
A nucleotide is a sugar, a base and a phosphate; DNA has deoxyribose and thymine, RNA ribose and uracil.
DNA is a double helix with A-T and G-C pairing, which makes replication possible.
Enzymes lower activation energy through an active site into which the substrate fits.
Enzyme rate depends on temperature, pH, substrate concentration and enzyme concentration, and is reduced by inhibitors.

questions.prompt: The bond joining two amino acids is called a:
questions.explanation: A peptide bond forms between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another.

questions.prompt: Which base is present in RNA but absent from DNA?
questions.explanation: Uracil replaces thymine in RNA, pairing with adenine in the same way.

questions.prompt: A non-competitive inhibitor reduces enzyme activity by:
options: Changing the shape of the active site
questions.answer: Changing the shape of the active site
questions.explanation: It binds away from the active site and alters its shape, so more substrate cannot overcome the inhibition.

questions.prompt: The structural polysaccharide of the arthropod exoskeleton is:
questions.explanation: Chitin is a polymer of N-acetylglucosamine forming the tough exoskeleton of insects and crustaceans.

questions.prompt: The three components of a nucleotide are a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and a __________ group.
questions.explanation: The phosphate is esterified to the sugar and gives the nucleic acid backbone its charge.

questions.prompt: The loss of a protein’s three-dimensional shape by heat or extreme pH, with loss of function, is called __________.
questions.explanation: The peptide bonds remain intact but the higher levels of structure are lost.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a monosaccharide and a disaccharide, giving an example of each.
questions.answer: A monosaccharide is the simplest carbohydrate and cannot be hydrolysed into smaller sugars; it consists of a single sugar unit such as glucose with the formula C6H12O6, and it is the form used directly in respiration. A disaccharide is formed when two monosaccharides join by a glycosidic bond in a condensation reaction with the loss of a water molecule, and it can be hydrolysed back into its two units; sucrose, formed from glucose and fructose, is the example, being the sugar transported in plants and found in cane sugar.
questions.explanation: Definition of each, the condensation link between them, and an example of each with its components.

questions.prompt: Explain why lipids store more energy per gram than carbohydrates.
questions.answer: Lipids contain a much higher proportion of carbon and hydrogen atoms relative to oxygen than carbohydrates do, and a lower proportion of oxygen. The long hydrocarbon chains of fatty acids are therefore highly reduced molecules, and oxidising the carbon to carbon dioxide and hydrogen to water releases a large amount of energy. Carbohydrates already carry more oxygen, so they are partly oxidised before they are metabolised and yield less energy per gram. In practical terms the complete oxidation of a lipid releases about nine kilocalories per gram against about four for a carbohydrate, and lipids also release metabolic water when oxidised, which is why they suit desert animals and seeds.
questions.explanation: The higher proportion of carbon and hydrogen and lower oxygen, the degree of reduction, and the kilocalorie figures.

questions.prompt: State the two rules of base pairing in DNA.
questions.answer: Adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine, so that a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine. The A-T pair is held by two hydrogen bonds while the G-C pair is held by three, which makes G-C pairs slightly more resistant to separation and gives regions rich in them a higher melting point. Because of this specificity each strand determines the sequence of its partner and can serve as a template during replication.
questions.explanation: A with T, G with C, with the hydrogen bond numbers and the template consequence.

questions.prompt: Describe the four levels of protein structure and explain why the tertiary level determines enzyme function.
questions.answer: The primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain, held together by peptide bonds formed during condensation; it is determined by the gene and, being a sequence, it contains all the information needed for the later folding. The secondary structure is the local folding of the chain into regular patterns — the right-handed alpha helix and the beta pleated sheet — held by hydrogen bonds between the atoms of the peptide backbone rather than between side chains. The tertiary structure is the complete three-dimensional arrangement of one polypeptide, produced as the side chains interact: hydrogen bonds between polar groups, ionic bonds between oppositely charged R groups, disulphide bridges between the sulphur atoms of two cysteines, and hydrophobic interactions that gather non-polar side chains into the interior away from water. The quaternary structure arises where a protein consists of more than one polypeptide, as in the four subunits of haemoglobin or the three chains of collagen, held together by the same forces. Enzyme function depends on the tertiary level because the active site is a cleft whose shape is created by amino acids that may lie far apart in the sequence yet are brought together by folding; the precise geometry of that cleft is what lets the substrate bind and the reaction proceed. Denaturation disrupts the tertiary bonds while leaving the primary sequence intact, the active site deforms, and the enzyme loses catalytic activity — which is exactly why function follows shape.
questions.explanation: Each level with what it is and what holds it, then the argument that the active site is a product of tertiary folding and that denaturation proves the link.

questions.prompt: An enzyme reaction is run at increasing substrate concentrations, and the rate rises and then plateaus. Explain the plateau, and state what happens to the curve when a competitive inhibitor is added and when the enzyme concentration is raised.
questions.answer: The plateau occurs because enzyme molecules work one substrate molecule at a time, each passing through a cycle of binding, conversion and release. At low substrate concentration many active sites stand empty, so adding substrate increases the number of enzyme-substrate complexes formed per second and the rate rises in proportion. As substrate concentration continues to rise, a growing fraction of the enzyme is occupied at any instant, and the rate of increase slows. Eventually every active site is occupied nearly all of the time — the enzyme is saturated — and the reaction runs at its maximum velocity, Vmax, so adding more substrate changes nothing and the curve becomes horizontal. When a competitive inhibitor is added, it resembles the substrate and competes for the same active sites, so at each substrate concentration fewer productive complexes form and the rate is lower; because the inhibitor and substrate compete, raising the substrate concentration can out-compete it, so the curve rises more slowly but still reaches the same Vmax. When the enzyme concentration is raised instead, there are more active sites available at every substrate concentration, so the curve rises more steeply and reaches a higher Vmax, because the plateau was set by the number of enzyme molecules rather than by the substrate.
questions.explanation: Saturation explained through active-site occupancy, the competitive inhibitor lowering the rate but not Vmax, and more enzyme raising Vmax.

questions.prompt: A food sample is suspected to contain a lipid. Describe the chemical test you would perform and the expected result, and explain how the result distinguishes lipids from carbohydrates.
questions.answer: The test for a lipid is the emulsion test. The sample is first dissolved in alcohol, since lipids are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents, and the alcohol solution is then poured slowly into a tube of distilled water. A positive result is the appearance of a milky white emulsion or cloudiness that does not clear on standing, caused by tiny lipid droplets suspended in the water. A negative result gives a clear solution with no cloudiness. The test works because the triglyceride molecules are hydrophobic: their long fatty acid tails cannot interact with water, so when the alcohol that held them is diluted they separate as droplets rather than dissolving, and it is the scattering of light by those droplets that makes the emulsion look milky. Carbohydrates behave differently because their many hydroxyl groups form hydrogen bonds with water, so sugars and starch dissolve or stay dispersed and give no emulsion; a starch sample would instead give a blue-black colour with iodine. Distinguishing the classes therefore rests on solubility, which in turn rests on the balance of polar and non-polar parts of the molecules.
questions.explanation: Emulsion test procedure, the milky result, the hydrophobic explanation, and the contrast with carbohydrate solubility and the iodine test.
